title: Eight Weeks in the Waiting
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for husbands and wives who can't have children, and anyone who longed to be a parent. Hannah's prayer, the hard days, the losses no one saw, and a hope that tells the truth.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for anyone who wants a child and has watched the answer come back no, month after month or year after year. It's for the wife and for the husband, who often grieve this differently, for the one who lost a pregnancy few people knew about, and for the woman or man who is single and longed to be a parent. Whether you're still trying, have stopped, or never had the chance, the ache is real. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. It moves slowly on purpose, from Hannah's prayer, the strain on a marriage, the hard days, and the losses no one saw, down to the fear that God is keeping score, and then to decisions made together, a life that isn't on hold, and a hope that tells the truth. It won't promise you a child, because no one honestly can. Your longing isn't selfish, and your empty arms are not God's verdict on your faith or your worth.

It isn't a cure, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the real people who love you. I'm a pastor, not a doctor, and nothing here is medical or legal advice. If this grief has brought thoughts of not wanting to live, don't wait for any week: call or text 988 tonight. Walk the plan imperfectly, alone or side by side. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. Some weeks the question will be all you can manage, especially in the days after another month ends, and that counts.
careNote: If sadness hasn't lifted for weeks, or you've stopped sleeping, eating, or working, see a doctor or a licensed counselor, and for heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, or fainting in pregnancy or after a loss or procedure, call your doctor now, or 911 if it's severe. If you're afraid of your spouse, Find Help lists the Domestic Violence Hotline; in a crisis, call or text 988.

weeks.why: This grief has no funeral, and it starts over every few weeks, usually in private. Scripture doesn't treat it as small. In Hannah's story a wife weeps and will not eat, and the narrator says this went on "year after year" (1 Samuel 1:7). Her husband asked the wrong question, and the priest watched her lips move and decided she was drunk. She told him, "I have poured out my soul before the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:15). She did bear a son, and Scripture doesn't promise you her ending. It shows you her God, who heard a prayer made mostly of tears. A psalm that bears David's name opens, "How long, O LORD?" (Psalm 13:1), and asks how long four times before it asks for anything else. That is the question this grief asks every month, and Scripture lets you ask it to God's face.
weeks.practice: Each day, find five minutes alone and pray Psalm 13 aloud, as far as you honestly can. On the days you can't pray the last two verses, stop after the fourth; that is still a prayer. Then tell God in one plain sentence how today really went. If this grief has turned into thoughts of not wanting to live, call or text 988 tonight.

read.label: How to Practice Lament, on bringing God the complaint without softening it

tool.label: 1 Samuel 1 in the Study Bible, Hannah's story, with notes on the husband who misunderstood and the priest who misread her

weeks.reflection: What have I stopped saying to God about this, because I'm tired of hearing myself pray it?

weeks.focus: Grieving side by side, without blame
weeks.why: Infertility tests a marriage in new places. One of you wants to talk, the other wants to fix it or stop talking; one is ready for the next appointment, the other worn out. If the cause has been traced to one of you, that spouse may carry a private shame, and many husbands hide this grief as if it were a failure of manhood. Elkanah loved Hannah and asked her, "Am I not better to you than ten sons?" (1 Samuel 1:8), a kind question that missed her completely. When Rachel demanded children, Jacob, who loved her, answered in anger (Genesis 30:1-2), and grief set them on opposite sides. If you're afraid of your spouse, or the blame has turned into threats or control, set this week aside and call the National Domestic Violence Hotline, listed on Find Help, or 911 if you're in danger.
weeks.practice: Each day, ask your spouse how they're really doing this month, and listen without trying to fix it. Agree on a time to talk about this and a time to set it down, so it doesn't swallow every evening. If you can't talk without blaming each other, see a counselor together, as long as you're safe with each other. If you carry this without a spouse, tell one friend who can keep a confidence how this month really went.

read.label: How to Have a Weekly Marriage Check-In, on a short, protected conversation where you listen without fixing

tool.label: The Conflict Guide, which opens with the Domestic Violence Hotline for anyone afraid of their spouse, then gives couples who are safe with each other five steps for talking again

weeks.reflection: Where has this grief put me on the opposite side from someone I love, and what one gentle, honest sentence could I say to them?

weeks.focus: The hard days on the calendar
weeks.why: The announcements keep coming, at Thanksgiving, in the group chat, at church, at the shower. Mother's Day and Father's Day can become the hardest Sundays of the year, and in some churches the mothers stand to be applauded while you stay in your seat. You can love your friend and still be unable to hold her newborn this week, and feeling both doesn't make you a bad person. Envy is where the ache can turn hard, and Scripture doesn't hide that Rachel envied her sister (Genesis 30:1); bring that part to God too. Paul told the church in Rome, "Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15). That command runs in both directions. On the day of someone else's good news, you may be asked to rejoice, and you are also someone the church is asked to weep with.
weeks.practice: This week, mark the hard dates on your calendar: Mother's Day and Father's Day, a shower, the holiday table where someone always asks, a due date that came and went, the anniversary of a loss. For each, decide where you'll be and who will know. You may stay home, or sit near the back beside someone who knows and leave when you need to; a gift and a kind note can go to the shower without you. Each morning, pray one honest line about the day ahead.

read.label: Infertility and Childlessness, the Wisdom page, on a grief surrounded by announcements and telling safe people what helps and what wounds

tool.label: The Prayer Generator, with written prayers for strength for the morning of a hard day

weeks.reflection: Whose good news has been hardest for me to hear, and how could I love them honestly without pretending it doesn't hurt?

weeks.why: Some of you conceived and then lost the pregnancy, and the child you'd already begun to love was gone before most people knew there was a child at all. A miscarriage is a real loss however early it came, and so is your grief, though it's often carried in near silence. Some parents grieve hard and some are surprised by what they feel; neither is a failure of love. Husbands grieve these losses too, often quietly. Other losses never had a name: a month that ended in no, a call from the clinic, the child you pictured and never met. Psalm 139, which bears David's name, says to God, "You knit me together in my mother's womb" (Psalm 139:13). No child is hidden from him, however brief their life, and no grief you carry is hidden either.
weeks.practice: Each evening this week, write one line about a loss in this long wait that no one else saw, and pray it to God by name. If you've lost a pregnancy, give that loss a place too: name the baby if you want to, mark the date, and ask one person to remember it with you. For heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, or fainting in pregnancy or after a loss or procedure, call your doctor now, or 911 if it's severe.

read.label: Miscarriage and Pregnancy Loss, the Wisdom page, on the death of a child you loved before you ever held them

tool.label: A grief journal page to print, with room for what you miss, what you wish you could say, and an angry prayer

weeks.reflection: What loss in this long wait have I carried without anyone knowing, and who could I let know this week?

weeks.focus: The fear that God is keeping score
weeks.why: Under the grief lies a second weight, shame and the fear that God is keeping score. Part is old; when Rachel bore a son she said, "God has taken away my shame" (Genesis 30:23). Part is newer: many of us learned to schedule children, so a pregnancy that won't come feels like failure. And part the church laid on you. We made the family with children our picture of faithfulness, and some pulpits promise that enough faith opens a womb, which wounds twice: no child, then the blame. I'm a pastor and the father of five sons, so I stand inside that picture and that indictment. Scripture does say "the LORD had closed Hannah's womb" (1 Samuel 1:6). Where it names childlessness as a judgment, it says so and gives the reason (Genesis 20:18); of Hannah it says neither. No one may read a hidden sin off an empty nursery.
weeks.practice: Each day, write down one thing you've come to believe about yourself because of this: that God is punishing you, that your faith is too small, that you're less of a woman or less of a man. Then read Luke 1:5-7 and set Luke's words beside yours. If something in your past haunts you anyway, confess it to God by name and read Romans 8:1 aloud. Before the week ends, tell one person which of these beliefs has been loudest.

read.label: Where Is God in Infertility and Childlessness? On the lie that a closed womb is a verdict, and how the church has held the childless

tool.label: Luke 1 in the Study Bible, where a righteous couple had no children, with notes on why Luke names their faithfulness first

weeks.reflection: What have I believed God thinks of me because of this, and where did I first learn to believe it?

weeks.why: Sooner or later come the decisions: whether to begin treatment or keep going, how far, at what cost, whether to adopt, or whether to stop. Seeking a doctor's help isn't a lack of trust, and deciding to stop, if that time comes, isn't a lack of faith. Whether IVF is right for Christians, and on what terms, is a question faithful Christians answer differently; the care page sets out three positions in their strongest form and doesn't decide for you. Adoption sits close to the heart of the gospel, but it's a calling for some, neither a consolation prize nor a cure. It doesn't erase the grief for the child you couldn't conceive, and no child should be asked to fill that space. If you aren't drawn to it, that isn't selfishness. Whoever lacks wisdom is told to "ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault" (James 1:5).
weeks.practice: Each day, pray one sentence asking for wisdom about the next step. Before you take it, sit down, together if you're married, and write what you will and won't do: how many tries, how much money, what you believe about embryos, what you'll do if this round fails. If you're considering adoption, a donor, or a surrogate, talk to a lawyer who knows your state's family law before you sign anything. If you can't agree, take it to a counselor or a pastor you both trust.

read.label: We can't have children, the care page, on setting limits together, with its answers on IVF and adoption

tool.label: How do I know what God wants me to do? The care page for anyone afraid of choosing wrong, on what God has already said

weeks.reflection: What am I afraid will happen if I decide, and what is not deciding already costing me?

weeks.focus: A life that isn't on hold
weeks.why: Waiting can put a whole life on hold: the trip you won't book in case you're pregnant, the job you won't take, the friends you've let drift. Hope can keep its place without taking every room in the house. Isaiah expected the eunuch, who could have no children, to say of himself, "I am but a dry tree" (Isaiah 56:3), and God answered with a place in his own house and "a name better than that of sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:5). Told that his mother and brothers were outside, Jesus looked at the people around him and said, "Here are My mother and My brothers!" (Mark 3:34). In the church, a person without children was never meant to be a guest. Your life may come to include other people's children, as a mentor, an aunt, or an uncle, or it may not; neither is a lesser life.
weeks.practice: Choose one thing this week that belongs to the life you have now, not the one you're waiting for: book the trip, call the friend you've let drift, say yes to the work you've held off. Each day, read Isaiah 56:3-5 slowly. Once this week, share a meal with someone from church who isn't in your season of life.

read.label: Why Does the Bible Call the Church a Family? On a household where kinship runs deeper than blood

tool.label: Isaiah 56 in the Study Bible, where God promises the eunuch, who could have no children, a name better than sons and daughters

weeks.reflection: What have I put on hold until this is settled, and what would it mean to start living that part of my life now?

weeks.focus: A hope that tells the truth
weeks.why: God has not promised you a child, and anyone who says he has is promising more than God has. Hebrews honors people who "died in faith, without having received the things they were promised" (Hebrews 11:13), and the Bible never explains why one couple conceives and another doesn't. What it does promise is enough to stand on. Paul writes that believers groan as they wait for "the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23), and that when we don't know how to pray, the Spirit "intercedes for us with groans too deep for words" (Romans 8:26). Every Christian lives in that waiting, and it ends in resurrection, whatever happens before then. Hannah's face changed after she prayed, before anything had changed in her body (1 Samuel 1:18). A hope like that doesn't need a guaranteed ending, so it can be carried for years.
weeks.practice: Look back over these weeks and write on a card the two or three practices that actually helped, with when you'll keep them. Each morning this week, pray Psalm 13 again, all six verses if you can and the first four if you can't. Before the week ends, tell someone who has walked with you where your hope stands now, and ask them to check on you in a month.

read.label: How to Find Hope When Nothing Changes, on a hope that doesn't depend on the circumstance finally turning

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, to choose a few practices you can keep on an ordinary week

weeks.reflection: What has God actually promised me, and how would my hope change if I let my weight rest there?
